diluted to a final working concentration of 0.2-0.5 μg per test. Data were collected and analyzed
using flow cytometer (BD LSRFortessa™ X-20) and FlowJo software (10.6.2).

In vitro antibacterial assessment
SEM (Sigma 300) was used to observe the bacteria (S. aureus and E. coli) morphology after
different treatments. The ROS level of bacteria was assessed using the bacterial ROS detection kit
(BestBio) and imaged under an upright microscope (Leica DM6 B). Spread plate assay was
adopted to evaluate the antibacterial effect. In brief, prepared bacterial suspensions (15 μL, 107
mL-1) were added to the pre-treated 24-well cell plate and received different group treatments.
Bacterial suspensions were harvested with sterile PBS (1 mL) and diluted approximately 800-fold.
Bacterial survival was determined by enumerating CFUs after 18 h of incubation on agar plates.
All experiments were conducted in triplicate, and survival rates were calculated as: survival rate
(%) = (C / C ) × 100%. C and C denote colony numbers in control and treated groups, respectively.
0 0
In addition, bacterial suspensions subjected to different treatments were passed through 0.22 μm
filters, and the concentration of bacterial protein leakage was calculated by BCA protein
quantification kit (Beyotime). To evaluate bactericidal efficacy, each sample was tested using a
viability/cytotoxicity assay kit (L6060, UElandy) and observed under an upright microscope
(Leica DM6 B, Germany). The bacterial reduction rate (%) was calculated as: reduction rate (%)
= (N / N ) × 100%. N and N denote the total and the dead bacterial count, respectively.
0 0

Study in diabetic wound model
For establishment of the diabetic models, animals were fasted for more than 12 h prior to STZ
administration. The rat diabetes model was induced by a single i.p. injection of STZ (50 mg kg-¹),
while the mouse diabetes model was established through five consecutive i.p. injections of STZ
(50 mg/kg). Blood glucose levels in all animals were measured twice a week using a glucometer
(Accu-Chek®) for 4 weeks after STZ injection. Successful modeling of diabetic animals was
defined as randomized glucose >16.7 mmol L-1 for two consecutive readings. After modeling, the
diabetic animals were anesthetized (1% pentobarbital sodium) and a back full-thickness skin
wound (2 cm diameter for rats and 8 mm diameter for mice) was created using a round punch
under aseptic conditions. The successfully modeled animals were randomly divided into six
groups: Control (PBS), LIFU, Gel, BT@Gel, BT@Gel+LIFU and BT-dNO@Gel+LIFU (n = 5
rats per group). The dose of BT or BT-dNO was 0.3 mg mL-1, LIFU parameters were 1.5 W cm-2,
50% duty cycle, 1.0 MHz and 120 s duration, and freshly prepared gel bandage was replaced every
other day to ensure sustained bioactive ion release. Wound images were acquired at predetermined
time points to evaluate the healing process. The wound closure rate was calculated based on the
following formula: wound closure (%) = (A - A) / A × 100%. A and A denote the original
0 t 0 0 t
wound area and the wound area at different time point, respectively.

Study in rat diabetic infected wound model
For diabetic rat with infected wound model, after experiencing the above STZ-induced diabetes
and establishing the back skin defect, the S. aureus or E. coli suspension (150 μL, 1 × 108 CFU
mL-1) was spread onto the wounds. Wound infection was confirmed 24 h after inoculation by
routine swab culture followed by spread plate analysis on solid agar. The successfully modeled
rats were than randomly allocated into groups based on the aforementioned grouping (n = 5 rats
per group). Wound healing was monitored by photographing and measuring wound areas at
predetermined time points, while bacterial infection was assessed by swab culture and spread plate
methods on days 7 and 14.

Study in rat DNP model
For DNP model, the diabetic rats were first constructed according to the aforementioned method,
and the blood glucose status and behavioral changes were monitored. One month after injection,
rats with blood glucose levels >16.7 mmol L-1 and 50% PWT decreased more than 50% from
baseline indicated successful establishment of the DNP model. The DNP rats were anesthetized
(1% pentobarbital sodium) and a right foot full-thickness skin wound (8 mm diameter) was created
to establish the DFU model on day 0. The successfully modeled DNP combined with DFU rats
were randomly divided into six groups to receive the different treatments described above (n = 5
rats per group). The wound healing process and behavioral changes were monitored during
treatment.

Behavior tests
Mechanical nociception was determined using the Von Frey filaments by measuring paw
withdrawal responses to stimulation on the plantar surface of rat hind paw. Prior to routine testing,
each rat received a 30 min adaptation period on pain test mesh rack covered with Plexiglas
chambers. Adaptation was confirmed when the rat entered a quiet state with reduced voluntary
activities. Von Frey filaments of increasing force (1.4-26 g) were applied vertically to the central
plantar surface of the hind paw for 6-8 s. Paw withdrawal or licking was considered a positive
response, proceeding to the next lower-force filament, whereas failure to respond led to use the
next higher-force filament. The testing sequence was continued until four measurements were
collected after the first behavioral change, or until four successive negative responses or five
successive positive responses occurred. The 50% PWT (denoted in grams, g) was determined by
the up-down method of Dixon. Hot nociception was evaluated using hot plate test, specifically by
timing the latency of rapid thumping of the hind paw, hind paw-licking or jumping. Rats were
placed on the plate at RT for 30 min prior to formal testing. Subsequently, they were transferred
to a hot plate heated to 55 °C for observation. Measurements were conducted three times with a
15 min interval between each session and a 30 s cut-off time is set to avoid foot burns.

Isolation, cultivation and experimentation of DRG neurons
DRG neurons were isolated from rat embryos on day 18 of embryonic development and
immediately plated into cold DMEM medium. Then DRGs were then washed with DMEM
medium and digested with an enzyme mixture solution (DNase Ⅰ, trypsin and collagenase) at 37°C
for 20 min until cell detachment. Next, the cell suspension was filtered with cell strainer (100 μm)
and purified with Percoll. DRG neurons were resuspended in Neurobasal medium with 2% B-27
(Gibco) and cultured in an incubator.
For IF staining of TRPV1, DRGs were pre-seeded in confocal dishes (1 × 105 cells per well) and
subjected to different treatments. After PBS washing, the neurons were fixed with 4%
polyformaldehyde (PFA) at RT (15 min), and incubated in QuickBlock™ Blocking Buffer
(Beyotime, P0260) for 15 min. After triple washing by PBS, the specimens were incubated with
anti-TRPV1 primary antibody (diluted at 1:200, ABclonal, A8564) overnight at 4 °C, and then
incubated with Alexa Fluor® 488-conjugated secondary antibody (diluted at 1:800, Abcam,
ab150077) for 1 h at RT. Before observed under CLSM, the nuclei were stained with DAPI.
For calcium imaging, DRG neurons were inoculated into confocal dishes (1 × 105 cells per well)
and cultured until cell attachment. Fluo-4 AM (4 μM) was added to the serum-free DMEM medium
and co-incubated with neurons in the dark at 37 °C for 30 min. Neurons were then washed and
treated with Cap or BT-dNO@Gel in culture media. LIFU stimulation was carried out at 1.5 W cm-
2 for 30 s. The fluorescence images were captured using CLSM.

Histological analysis
To assess wound closure status, epidermal regeneration, immune infiltration and analgesia
mechanism, the rats skin tissues, L4/L5 DRGs and spinal cord dorsal horn were harvested and
fixed in 4% PFA for 20 min-1 h, followed by dehydration and paraffin embedding. Tissue sections
of 5 μm thickness were cut using a microtome for histological analysis. Re-epithelialization and
collagen deposition were evaluated by H&E staining, Masson’s trichrome staining and
immunohistochemistry staining of collagen I (dilution at 1: 500, Abcam, ab270993, clone no.
EPR24331-53) and collagen III (dilution at 1: 200, Abcam, ab7778). ROS levels within wound
tissue were assessed using DHE dye (Beyotime, S0064S). For IF staining, tissue sections
underwent a 90 min blocking step followed by overnight incubation with the primary antibody at
4°C and a 2 h incubation with the secondary antibody at RT. Prior to imaging (Leica DM3000 and
Zeiss Axio Imager Z1), cell nuclei were stained with DAPI. Primary antibodies involved in
experiment include Ki67 (dilution at 1: 500, Abcam, ab15580), CD31 (dilution at 1: 100, Abcam,
ab222783, clone no. EPR17260-263), α-SMA (dilution at 1: 500, Bioss, bsm-33187M, clone no.
3F9), K14 (dilution at 1: 100, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA5-11599, clone no. LL002), vimentin
(dilution at 1: 1000, ABclonal, A19607, clone no. ARC0086), CD68 (dilution at 1:100, Abcam,
ab283654, clone no. EPR23917-164), Arg1 (dilution at 1: 200, CST, #93668, clone no. D4E3M),
CD206 (dilution at 1: 500, Abcam, ab64693), CD86 (dilution at 1: 200, ABclonal, A16805),
Na 1.8 (dilution at 1: 2000, Abcam, ab307817, clone no. EPR25132-222), TRPV1(dilution at 1:
v
200, ABclonal, A8564), GFAP (dilution at 1: 500, CST, #3670, clone no. GA5), Iba-1 (dilution at
1: 200, CST, #17198, clone no. E4O4W) and CGRP (dilution at 1: 200, CST, #14959, clone no.
D5R8F).

Transcriptome sequencing
Total RNA was isolated from wound tissues using TRIzol reagent at the end of treatment. RNA
quality and quantification were tested using Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer and ND-2000 NanoDrop
spectrophotometer. Library construction and sequencing were performed on an Illumina HiSeq
2000 system. Differential expression analysis among the naive, control and BT-dNO@Gel+LIFU
groups was analyzed using DESeq2 (v1.4.5) with a significance threshold of Q value ≤ 0.05.
KEGG and GO enrichment analysis of DEGs were conducted using Phyper based on the
hypergeometric test, and statistical significance was corrected by Bonferroni adjustment with a Q
value threshold of ≤ 0.05.

Real-time quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-qPCR)
Total RNA was extracted with the Eastep Total RNA Extraction Kit (Promega). Complementary
DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from total RNA using the HiScript® II First Strand cDNA
Synthesis Kit (Vazyme Biotech Co., Ltd.). RT-qPCR analysis was performed with SYBR Green
PCR Master Mix (Biotechnology), and gene expression was normalized to Gapdh. Primers were
ordered from Sangon Biotech. The primer sequences for Calca and Gapdh used were as follows51:
Rat_Calca forward primer: 5’- GAAATGCCACCTTTTGACAGTG -3’,
Rat_Calca reverse primer: 5’- TGGATGCTCTCATCAGGACAG -3’,
Rat_Gapdh forward primer: 5’- AGGTCGGTGTGAACGGATTTG -3’,
Rat_Gapdh reverse primer: 5’- TGTAGACCATGTAGTTGAGGTCA -3’.

Statistical analysis
All experiments were performed with at least three biological replicates. Quantitative data were
presented as mean ± SD. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software
(version 8.2.1), IBM SPSS software (version 27.0.1.0), and OriginPro 2024 software. A two-tailed
unpaired Student’s t-test was applied for comparisons between two groups, whereas one-way
ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test was used for multiple-group comparisons. Statistical
differences were denoted as ns, not significant, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 and
****P<0.0001.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this paper, the authors prepared a low intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU)-activated piezoelectric gel bandage for DFU wound repair and evaluated the therapeutic efficacy in a rat model of diabetic neuropathic pain. In general, the paper is well organized with good novelty. Some revisions are required as follows.
1. BT-dNO@Gel designed in this study can produce both NO and ROS. In this regard, could the release of NO be precisely controlled because NO is short-lived radical demonstrating dual effect at different dose? At least, some discussion on this point is needed. Next, the NO can react with ROS to generate peroxynitrite (ONOO) with high level toxicity. Have the authors notice the production of ONOO and its effect on the wound healing?
2. The authors mentioned that ROS produced by LIFU activated piezoelectric catalytic reaction has bactericidal effect, but excessive accumulation of ROS may lead to cell damage, oxidative stress and even delayed wound healing. Therefore, it is recommended to detect the production of ROS in vivo, and provide relevant discussion.
3. Mechanistically, the relieved neuropathic pain is ascribed to the desensitizing of TRPV1 receptor by the BT-dNO@Gel. Relevant experimental results are required to verify this hypothesis Are there other possible mechanisms for pain relief that have not been considered?
4.In the current version, the gene expression was evaluated through transcriptome analysis. It would be helpful to validate these changes by other experimental methods, such as qPCR or Western blot? In addition, are there experimental data to support the functional significance of these gene expression changes?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper investigated the effects of low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU)-activated piezoelectric gel dressing (BT-dNO@Gel) on diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) treatment, exploring its impact on immune homeostasis and neuropathic pain relief. The paper presents a novel concept of using LIFU-activated piezoelectric gel dressing for DFU treatment. The experimental design is reasonable, and the result analysis is relatively sufficient. However, the presented work raises several critical concerns that need to be addressed before considering it for publication.
(1) The introduction section provides a detailed introduction to the pathogenesis and treatment status of DFU, but there is insufficient elaboration on the current research status of the application of piezoelectric materials and LIFU in wound healing. It is recommended to supplement relevant content.
(2) As the author stated, Under LIFU irradiation, the outer NONOate of the BT-dNO decomposes to release NO. However, NO, as a bioactive molecule, has various important roles and functions in the human body and organisms. The effects of different NO concentrations are very different. When NO concentration <1-30 nM, it could promote cell survival and proliferation, when >1000 nM, it could kill bacterial bioflms. The authors should add relevant experiments to reflect the specific concentration curve of NO released by this hydrogel under US irradiation.
(3) Additionally, under LIFU irradiation, the inner BT core would produce an unbalanced charge on their surface and undergo cascading redox reaction process, which leads to the generation of ROS and a localized electric field. The types of ROS include various species such as superoxide anions (O2-), hydroxyl radicals (• OH), etc. There are differences in the bactericidal performance of different ROS. Please supplement Electron spin resonance to detect the various ROS produced by BT dNO.
(4) BTdNO@Gel Bandages have good in vitro bactericidal ability. As far as we know, high concentrations of NO and ROS both contribute to the bactericidal effect. In this process, are the two synergistically antibacterial or do they rely solely on LIFU-triggered ROS generation?
(5) BT@Gel and BT-dNO@Gel can lead to the rupture of bacterial film and the leakage of a large amount of protein, resulting in the death of bacteria. Please supplement the electron microscope images of bacteria to show the above process more directly.
(6) As mentioned in the paper, infection is one of the major obstacles to wound healing in diabetes, and dressings with antibacterial activity will help block pathogen invasion and promote wound recovery, but the authors only demonstrated that this bandage has a satisfactory bactericidal effect against Staphylococcus aureus. The antibacterial effect of gram-negative bacteria is also crucial for diabetic wound healing, so please supplement the relevant experiments.
(7) As shown in FIG. 6a-6d, there was a decrease in M1 macrophages and an increase in M2 macrophages in the BT-dNO@Gel+LIFU group. What is the mechanism for regulating the polarization of macrophages? Is it related to NO?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Li and colleagues report the development of a piezoelectric gel bandage activated by low-intensity focused ultrasound to aid in diabetic wound repair and neuropathic pain relief.
The authors use a series of immunohistochemical, physiological and molecular biological assays to test the ability of this hydrogel formulation to heal diabetic wounds. This addresses a significant problem, since diabetic foot ulcers are notoriously painful and difficult to treat. Additionally, this formulation represents a multifunctional approach, incorporating strategies that have been developed elsewhere and now applied to diabetic neuropathy.
However, there are several issues with the manuscript which curtailed my enthusiasm:
1. Line 64 appears to imply the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin has abuse liability. Presumably this refers to a now-deleted mention of opioids, because there is no evidence I’m aware of that capsaicin or TRPV1 modulators in general exhibit abuse liability.
2. The rationale for settling on electrical stimulation could be better articulated. For example, citing evidence that the approach has potential, talk about the potential mechanisms of action and then outline the current difficulties/limitations of this approach that their novel formulation will circumvent.
3. The authors mention that the device liberates ROS without first mentioning the therapeutic potential of this approach. Fig. 1 appears to suggest the benefit of ROS is derived solely from being bactericidal, but ROS can be directly pro- and anti-inflammatory also, this should be addressed.
4. Couldn’t the beneficial effects of the formulation also be mediated by NO-driven vasodilation? This doesn’t seem to have been considered.
5. Fig. 1 is a graphical abstract – either include it as such, or move it to the end of the results section as a tentative schematic, or remove it.
6. It was not clear if the durability of NO mobilization and/or NO release kinetics were tested in vivo. In other words, is there evidence that LIFU stimulation several days after application is still able to liberate physiologically relevant quantities of NO/ROS?
7. The study would benefit from comparison to standard wound dressings/antibiotics, or standard systemic dosing with a nitric oxide donor, such as nitroglycerin or sodium nitroprusside.
8. Fig. 3 seems to show NO release/ROS production in vitro over the course of 2-3 minutes. What evidence is there that LIFU can be used to generate sustained NO release/ROS in vivo? Presumably a shifting of macrophage phenotype requires more than a few minutes of enhanced ROS.
9. Could the authors use L-NAME to block NO and test whether the effects on HUVEC proliferation/migration are blocked?
10. Is >16.7mM on non-fasted rats a benchmark for diabetes following STZ that has precedent?
11. The statistical tests, particularly in Fig. 5 (unpaired t-test), seems inappropriate. Two-way, repeated measures ANOVA would be more appropriate for Fig. 5D for example.
12. The authors do not directly test the effect of this formulation on macrophages in vitro to establish if the beneficial effects on wound healing are a direct effect of the formulation on macrophage function. It’s possible there is an association here, but the chief driver could be the bactericidal activity which dampens innate inflammation and results in a less-pro-inflammatory microenvironment and fewer M1-like macrophages being present.
13. Fig. 6 – requires additional evidence to localize the iNOS and Arg1 staining with a known macrophage marker (F4/80, CD68).
14. Which cells are Ki67 positive? It would bolster the claims being made regarding growth factors if there was a concordant increase in proliferation of the target cell type (keratinocytes/vascular endothelial cells).
15. Why wasn’t more testing of wound healing done in the hindpaw DFU model?
16. In the pain behavior testing, there is no group where gel formulations are delivered to non-diabetic rats, where presumably there would be no effect on mechanical sensitivity.
17. PC-12 cells are not an ideal model of sensory neurons in this context, especially when there may be effects on multiple sensory neuron channels that PC12 cells do not express, and the team show they can access lumbar DRG from rats for other downstream applications.
18. Figure 8e doesn’t look like plasma membrane staining at all, which would be expected for a functional ion channel.
19. Why is the effect size in the pain behavior testing very small – approximately 15% reversal versus naïve controls?
20. The IHC evidence for activity of TRPV1 sensory neurons is generally weak. For example, the interpretation that a TRPV1+ cell is less likely to be Fos+ doesn’t necessarily mean that reduced TRPV1 activity is responsible for this.
21. The TRPV1 staining pattern in DRGs is unconvincing, because it looks to be labeling most neurons rather than a subset of neurons, and there is an unexpected signal from what looks like nuclei as well.
22. What was the skin RNA-seq compared against as control. This is important to explain clearly in order to know if the differentially-expressed genes can be ascribed to LIFU, ROS production, etc.
23. Using PC12 cells to illustrate the promotion of CGRP expression/release is not optimal. The IHC for CGRP in Fig. 9 does not resemble cutaneous nerves, nor is there any co-staining with a neuronal marker (e.g. beta 3-tubulin, PGP9.5) to aid in identifying the cells responsible for the CGRP immunoreactivity.
24. There are also no experiments attempting to interfere with CGRP signaling in macrophages to confirm that this signaling is necessary for the formulation’s beneficial effects.
25. Fig. S18 – I struggle to interpret whether the immunostaining is specific or if there is a high degree of background.
Minor points:
The wording of the introduction could benefit from editing to optimize grammar and word choices.
Macrophages can adopt a stereotypical profile of M1 or M2 in vitro, but this is broadly considered to be an oversimplification when discussing the spectrum of macrophage function in vivo. Where possible, that terminology should be avoided, or at the very least acknowledge its limitations.
The transcript name for CGRP should be styled Calca (italicized) rather than "CGRP."
Results section, page 224: it was not clear why ROS green fluorescence should be expected. I think some explanation of the experimental design is missing in this part.
Biosafety supplementary figures at the end does not form a logical narrative flow and should be moved closer to the initial characterization of the formulation.
There needs to be more emphasis on the incidence of DFU infection in the introduction. It wasn’t clear before reading the results that this was part of the formulation’s intended activity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In the manuscript titled low intensity focused ultrasound-activated piezoelectric gel bandage for diabetic wound repair and neuropathic pain relief,' Li et al. report that the of BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU significantly promoted diabetic skin wound healing in a sterile or bacteria infection environment. The proposed mechanism involves macrophage polarisation, desensitisation of TRPV-1 nociceptors and the produce of ROS against invasive pathogens. Furthermore, the treatment may promote the release of CGRP from sensory neurons, which in turn contributes to macrophage polarisation. While the therapeutic efficacy of BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU in accelerating diabetic wound closure is acknowledged, the manuscript raised several major concerns regarding experimental design and data interpretation:
1. In the most statistical analysis, the authors included more than two groups in the experiments but conducted two-tailed unpaired student’s t-test. This approach is not appropriate for analysing the data with more than two groups in the experimental design. The authors should reanalyse data by using a one-way ANOVA or two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests for most of the figures to ensure proper statistical analysis and interpretation of the results.
2. In figure 4, the authors investigated the effects of BT-dNO@Gel with LIFU only on HUVEC. However, in the proliferation phase of wound healing processes, keratinocytes and fibroblast are also critical for promoting skin wound closure. The authors should perform the migration assay and cytotoxicity assay on these two cell types to understand whether BT-dNO@Gel with LIFU could directly affect keratinocyte and fibroblast cell growth and proliferation. Additionally, given the gel was applied immediately right after the skin punch, the immune cell responses, which are important for skin wound healing in the early of phase, would be affected by BT-dNO@Gel and required for further investigation.
3. In line 232-235, the authors stated that “Of note, the LIFU-triggered ROS generation from BT-dNO@Gel indeed affected bacteria survival but not HUVECs, probably due to the fact that the respiratory chain of eukaryotic cells is located in intracellular mitochondria, which is more resistant to external ROS interference than bacteria.” Please cite relevant references to justify their statement.
4. In the method, the authors described using a single ip injection of STZ to induce diabetes in a rat model. Two weeks post-injection, they performed the skin injury procedure and harvested the tissue two weeks post the injury. This implies that tissues harvesting occurs four weeks after the single injection of STZ.
Since that STZ induced diabetes and hyperglycaemia in rats may not be persistent for extended period, it is crucial for the authors to measure blood glucose levels weekly throughout the experimental period to confirm that hyperglycaemia persisted up to four weeks following the single injection of STZ. Additionally, the authors should clarify whether blood glucose levels were measured in a fasting or non-fasting state and provide these details in the method section to enhance the reproducibility and reliability of study.
5. In the animal work, the authors conducted 120s (50 % duty circle) of LIFU at the tissue injury site where the BT-dNO@Gel was delivery every other day. It implies this regime only allowed the gel to generate the current for 120 seconds every 48 hours. This raises a concern that such LIFU regime may result in the production of ROS and the release of NO for only a brief two-minute period, potentially limiting the therapeutic effects. To address this, the authors should evaluate the extent of ROS and NO generation at the wound site several hours post LIFU applications. This would help confirm whether the therapeutic effect of BT-dNO@Gel is sustained or merely transient following stimulation.
6. In line 260, the authors stated that “Digital photos and quantitative analysis of the wound sites showed that all the gel groups containing different formulations facilitated healing process to some extent compared to the control rats with significantly delayed wound healing, which can be attributed to well-adherent hydrogels providing a suitable matrix-like environment for fibroblast proliferation and epidermal regeneration (Fig. 5b-d).” However, there is no data or results to directly support that fibroblasts proliferation in vivo in this model. Please consider removing this statement or conduct relevant experiments, such us immunostaining, such as Ki67 and fibroblast markers, to support their points.
7. In line 269, the authors described that “In contrast to the immature granulation tissue, local inflammatory cell infiltration and incomplete epidermal bridging in the control group, the gel-containing groups had abundant neoplastic granulation tissue in the wound center with fewer inflammatory cells and increased epidermal viability, especially in BT-dNO@Gel+LIFU group (Fig. 5e-g). However, the authors did not provide the data to support how they identified inflammatory cell infiltration into the tissue site. The authors should perform experiments, such as immunostaining of pro-inflammatory immune markers, to identify and evaluate the extent of pro-inflammatory cell infiltration to the skin wound.
8. In figure 5, the excessive collagen disposition observed at the wound at the later timepoint (day 14) could suggest a contribute to scar formation and fibrosis, which are typically detrimental to skin wound healing. Could the authors clarify why they consider a larger collage area in the G6 groups at day 14 to be beneficial for skin wound healing? Additionally, it would be helpful to discuss whether the quality and organization of the collagen (e.g., alignment, type I vs. type III ratio) were assessed, as these factors are critical in determining whether collagen deposition supports regenerative healing or leads to fibrosis.
9. In figure 6a-d, the authors demonstrated a reduced number of iNOS+ cells and an increased large number of Arginase+ cells in the BT-dNO@Gel+LIFU-treated skin wounds, suggesting that the treatment regulates macrophage polarisation. However, macrophages are not the sole source of iNOS and arginase-1. The authors should perform IHC co-staining of F480 (or any macrophage makers) with iNOS, as wells F480 with Arginase on the same tissue sections to confirm that the observed changes in iNOS and Argainse-1 expression occurs in macrophages rather than in other cell types. Besides, it is not annotated in the manuscript which part of the skin wound was represented in the in Figure 6a and c. Were those images taken from the granulation tissue or the edges of the wound? Additionally, since immune cells are not evenly distributed across the tissue injury site, the authors should capture multiple images from a single tissue section. Quantification and averaging the positive staining cells from these images provide a more accurate representation of the number of positive staining cells. Alternatively, using flow cytometry to evaluate immune cell population in the wound is encouraging. In the figure 6e, f and g, there are no details of antibodies of TNFa and IL-6, IL-10 include in this manuscript. And given that they are detected by using immunostaining, the data presented as the intensity by percentage is puzzling. Please add all details to clarify how the quantification of the staining was conducted. Moreover, given that the backgrounds of staining images of TNFa, IL6 and IL10 are very high and inconsistent among all images as well as the result obtained from the IHC is semi-quantitive which cannot represent the condition in the entire skin wound. Using ELISA to detect these cytokines are required. There are same issues and concerns found in Figure 7g, h, i, j, k and Figure 9.
10. In figure 6k, it is not clear which cell type the ki67+ cells are. It could be immune cells, fibroblast, endothelial or keratinocytes. Since monocyte proliferation has been linked to chronic inflammation and delay skin wound healing in diabetic mice (PMID: 33443065), it is very crucial to perform co-staining of IHC to verify which cell types of these Ki67+ cells are. Lastly, in Figure 6h, the quantification of Ki67 should be presented as the percentage of Ki67+ cells out of the total cell number. It is not very common to quantify Ki67+ staining as the intensity. Could the authors clarify why they considered to present Ki67+ staining as the intensity?
11. Could the authors clarify whether the rats in Figure 8 received skin punch? Please add the skin punch procedure in the timeline presented in Figure 8a
12. In DNP model, mice received the treatment two weeks after the foot skin injury in which the skin wound was almost healing. Therefore, the BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU-indueced macrophage polarisation and CGRP release at the tissue injury observed in figure 8 might not contribute to wound regenerative repair. The authors should treat the skin wound right after the injury as they did in Figure 5 and observe macrophage polarisation, CGRP expression, and wound clousre to support their statement that “LIFU-mediated immune-nociceptor modulation strategy can orchestrate subcutaneous sensory nerve and M2 type macrophages interactions to achieve wound regenerative repair and analgesia.”
13. In Figures 8d–f, the authors used the PC-12 cell line as an in vitro model to investigate the direct effects of treatments on nociceptors. They measured the TRPV-1 levels in PC-12 cells and observed that the treatment reduced TRPV-1 expression in the presence of capsaicin. However, since the PC-12 cell line lacks proper characterization as a nociceptor neuron, the response observed here might not fully replicate the phenotype or function of native nociceptors. To address issue, the authors should use primary neuron cells isolated from DRG and detect TRPV1 expression in nociceptors, which can be identified by using nociceptor markers (PMID:26053673), after the treatment.
14. In the abstract, the authors state that piezoelectric current to desensitize TRPV1 nociceptor. However, in this manuscript, it is clearly showed that BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU induced the gel to generate ROS and NO. Since ROS and NO have been demonstrated to affect nociceptive pain (PMID: 17317010; PMID: 21723953), the effects of ROS and NO generated by the BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU on neurons should not be disregarded. The authors should investigate the role of these two factors on nociceptors. Additionally, if piezoelectric currents are indeed the primary factor causing TRPV1 nociceptor desensitization, the authors should measure the level of current generated by BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU to confirm whether it is sufficient to induce TRPV1 desensitization.
15. In figure 9f, the authors should use co-staining to confirm CGRP expression on nociceptors and Arg1 on macrophages. Particularly, the CGRP expression is almost co-localisation with Arg1, implying that CGRP might be expressed by macrophages (PMID: 20141542). Besides, the data obtained by using immunostaining approach is semi-quantitive. The authors should use ELISA to detect CGRP levels in the injury sites or in the corresponding DRG to support their statement.
16. The authors concluded that the BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU triggered CGRP release from nociceptors, therapy regulating macrophage polarisation tissue injury sites. However, based on their current data, BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU regulated directly affect HUVECs that have been demonstrated to affect macrophage activation (PMID: 23542777). Moreover, ROS and NO may also have impact on macrophage polarisation. To elucidate the critical role of CGRP, which might be upregulated by BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU, the authors should use genetic knockout (LysMCre-RAMP1floxed) animals or CGRP receptor antagonists (CGRP8-37, PMID: 1797334) on the skin wounds to confirm if BT-dNO@Gel_LIFU- promoted skin wound closure and M2 macrophage polarisation are disrupted.
Minor comments
1. In line 210, the authors stated that “ the blood cell hemolysis rate of BT-dNO was less than 5% within the safe range, suggesting its favorable hemocompatibility. Could the authors include the relevant reference to support this statement? Additionally, the bar graph in Figure S14 shows that 0.5mg/ml BT-dNO resulted in ~ 15% of hemolysis, which appears inconsistent with the statement in line 212 (5%). Could the authors verify the raw data and provide it in a table format instead of the bar graph to ensure accurate calculation of the percentage of homolysis?
2. In Figure S1, authors claims that the typical peak of C-C benzene ring at 1430 and 1565 cm-1 in the Raman spectra confirmed the existence of OH and pDA, respectively (fig. S1a, b). However, the peak of C-C benzene ring at 1430 cm-1 is only observed in BT-OH, not in the sample of BT-OH-pDA or BT- dNO. Could the authors clarify how to interpret the data and add these details in the result section?
3. In material and methods, line 560, how was PVA solution prepared?
4. In the line 658. the authors should clarify whether they replaced the gel every other days.
5. In figure 8b and c, should the label of x axis be “days after DNP”?

Response to Reviewers 1
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In this paper, the authors prepared a low intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU)-activated piezoelectric gel bandage for DFU wound repair and evaluated the therapeutic efficacy in a rat model of diabetic neuropathic pain. In general, the paper is well organized with good novelty. Some revisions are required as follows.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Nociceptive hypersensitivity and prolonged wound healing due to the interaction of peripheral
neuropathy and local immune disorders are key issues that need to be addressed in diabetic foot
ulcer (DFU) regenerative repair. Here, we present a low intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU)-
activated piezoelectric gel bandage for DFU wound repair and neuropathic pain relief. Acting as
an artificial “skin”, this self-powered, functionalized bandage not only temporarily shields tissue
from external environment, but also serves as a drug reservoir that can in situ release nitric oxide
upon LIFU to promote macrophage polarization, generate piezoelectric current to desensitize
TRPV1 nociceptor for on demand neuropathic pain relief and produce reactive oxygen species to
eliminate pathogens in male rodents. More importantly, this regimen can promote CGRP
neuropeptides release from sensory neurons to invigorate M2-like macrophages-mediated
protective cutaneous immunity. This LIFU-activated immune-nociceptor modulation strategy is
potentially applicable to other non-healing tissue regeneration.

---

## Introduction

Diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) are one of the most devastating complications of advanced diabetes
mellitus, with high disability and mortality rates, imposing heavy clinical and economic burdens
on society1. More than half of DFUs become infected, with about 20% of moderate to severe
infections leading to amputation, and the mortality after amputation exceeds 70% within 5 years
for all diabetic patients2,3. Long-term poor glycemic control in diabetic patients not only creates
persistent local inflammatory microenvironment that leads to immune disorders and vasculopathy,
but also causes peripheral neuropathy that results in abnormal foot sensation and protective
function deficiency4,5. These factors work together to make DFU highly susceptible to infection
and prolonged healing when exposed to adverse external factors. Current treatment of DFU mainly
focuses on systemic glycaemic control, microvascular recanalization, infection prevention and
local wound care, focus solely on healing effect but meet with rather limited success6–8. Thus,
developing comprehensive therapeutic regimens to simultaneously remodel immune homeostasis
and relieve peripheral nerve perception becomes indispensable for DFU management.

Diabetic wound microenvironment, as a local factor that participates in the pathogenesis and
continues to influence wound repair process with the support of systemic factors, consists mainly
of fibroblasts, immune cells, endothelial cells and various cytokines9,10. Of these, the immune
components play a key role in coordinating tissue healing. During chronic inflammation in
diabetes, macrophages are recruited to trauma site and release cytokines to modulate the immune
microenvironment11. Notably, macrophages are highly plastic and can be categorized into pro-
inflammatory state (M1-like macrophages) and anti-inflammatory state (M2-like macrophages)
depending on their response to different stimuli and functional phenotypes. M1-like macrophages,
activated by Th1 cytokines (e.g., γ-interferon, tumor necrosis factor-α) and exogenous danger
signals, exhibits strong cytotoxicity and pro-inflammatory properties, whereas M2-like
macrophages mainly exert anti-inflammatory and pro-cell proliferation effects12. Besides, studies
have shown that macrophages are involved in regeneration process of damaged peripheral nerves.
Modulation of macrophage polarization is expected to reverse the local inflammatory
microenvironment and support peripheral nerve repair to promote diabetic wound recovery13,14.

In addition to dysregulated immune microenvironment, abnormal pain perception caused by
peripheral neuropathy remains a non-neglectable problem affecting diabetic wound healing and
even patients' life quality15. Considering that the expression, transport and phosphorylation status
of ion channels within sensory neurons directly affect functional abnormalities, targeting
regulation of specific ion channels may remodel diabetic peripheral nerve perception. Transient
receptor potential vanilloid-1 (TRPV1), a receptor highly expressed in dorsal root ganglia (DRG)
neurons, is closely involved in pain process16. TRPV1 can be activated by deleterious chemical,
mechanical and thermal insults, triggering calcium influx, and, in turn, a cascade of events linked
to neurogenic inflammation and nociception17,18. Growing studies have validated long-term
analgesic efficacy of TRPV1 agonists or antagonists in diverse preclinical chronic pain models19,20.
However, currently available selective TRPV1 agonists such as capsaicin (Cap) have limited
clinical efficacy due to its local irritation such as stinging, burning, and erythema. Therefore,
enormous efforts have been devoted to developing efficacious TRPV1 agonist without the adverse
effects associated with Cap application.

Local electrical stimulation has been proven to successfully stimulate receptor internalization,
macrophage polarization and tissue regeneration; however, the application of implanted electrodes
remains restrictive due to side effects such as invasiveness, infection, and electrode breakage. A
self-powered therapeutic strategy based on physical principles thus offers an ideal solution21–23.
Barium titanate (BaTiO , BT), a representative piezoelectric material, converts acoustic
3
mechanical energy into electrical energy, enabling ultrasound (US)-driven wireless stimulation;
meanwhile, the piezoelectric catalytic process produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) to
participate in the wound healing process24. These materials exhibit micro-pressure-induced
polarization, dynamic built-in electric fields, and excellent biocompatibility25,26. Studies confirm
that US-triggered piezoelectric BT systems significantly shorten the healing cycle of bacterially
infected wounds and improve immune homeostasis27,28. Critically, the ROS generated by
piezoelectric catalysis need to be properly regulated to coordinate its dual role of antibacterial and
healing29–31. Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU), with its precise energy focusing capability,
avoids tissue damage and discomfort caused by excessive energy (e.g., significant suppression of
acute pain perception in the human dorsal anterior cingulate) while enhancing therapeutic
efficiency32. Therefore, the synergistic interaction between LIFU and piezoelectric materials
presents a promising strategy for achieving enhanced therapeutic outcomes.

Herein, we introduce a LIFU-activated piezoelectric gel (BT-dNO@Gel) bandage with immune
homeostasis modulation and neuropathic pain relief functions for comprehensive repair of diabetic
wounds. This self-powered system was composed of polyethyleneimine (PEI) and polyvinyl
alcohol (PVA) cross-linked hydrogel encapsulating piezoelectric BT nanoparticles with surface-
coated nitric oxide (NO) donor capable of sequentially releasing NO, generating ROS and
outputting localized direct current in response to LIFU stimulation. Firstly, the use of non-invasive
LIFU as a switch for precise spatiotemporal control avoided local damage or discomfort caused
by implanted electrodes or excessive incident energy. Secondly, the outer hydrogel layer possessed
favorable biocompatibility, adhesion, and mechanical flexibility to conformably fill complex
wound areas and effectively transmit US and electrical currents into deep regions. Finally, the
subsequent on-demand released NO synergistically with free radicals and piezoelectric currents
generated by BT mechanical deformation accelerates wound healing process through combating
pathogen infection, polarizing macrophages to M2-like phenotype, desensitizing TRPV1
nociceptor and releasing calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP). This LIFU-mediated immune-
nociceptor modulation strategy not only present a valuable approach for diabetic wound care, but
also hold great potential for other chronic or acute wounds.
